client: I've been really dreading this family reunion coming up next month. Ever since my cousin and I had that huge fight last year, just thinking about seeing her again makes my heart pound like crazy. I keep imagining all these awkward scenarios where we have to interact, and I'm not sure therapy can really help with something this messy.
therapist: It sounds like this reunion is bringing up both painful memories and a lot of worry for you. I notice your voice tightens when you talk about it—that tells me this situation feels both upsetting and draining for you. Let's look at those imagined scenarios together—are they predictions or fears?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, it’s definitely draining. I keep imagining how awkward it’s going to be—like, what if no one really talks to me or I end up sitting alone? I keep telling myself it’s just my anxiety, but it feels so real, like it’s definitely going to happen. I don’t know if it’s a prediction or a fear, but it’s hard to shake the feeling.
therapist: I hear how heavy this feels for you—your voice sounds tense and uncertain, like you’re carrying this worry with you. Let’s explore this: what evidence do you have that it *will* be awkward, and is there room for a different outcome? Sometimes our fears feel so vivid, but they’re not always the full story.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I don’t have concrete evidence it’ll be awkward—it’s just this gut feeling that’s hard to shake. I keep imagining everyone judging me or me saying something stupid. It feels so real, even though I know it’s probably exaggerated. But it’s hard to believe it could go differently when I’ve felt this way before.
therapist: Your voice sounds both hesitant and weighed down—like part of you knows these fears might be exaggerated, but they still feel so convincing. That tension between what you *know* and what you *feel* is really common with anxiety—let’s look at those past experiences you mentioned. Were there moments when things actually went better than you expected?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about things sometimes turning out better than expected, but it's hard to trust that. Just last week I avoided meeting up with friends because I was convinced I'd say something awkward or they wouldn't really want me there. Now I keep seeing their social media posts together and feel even worse. 

The thing is, I can point to a few times where things went okay, but my brain always focuses on the times things went badly instead. Like that one time I actually did go out and someone made a comment about me being quiet - now that's all I remember, not the other times people seemed happy to see me.
therapist: I hear how fast and urgent your voice gets when you talk about these moments—it’s like your brain zeroes in on the negative memories with such intensity. That one comment about being quiet seems to weigh so heavily, even though you *do* remember other times going well. What would it feel like to gently redirect that focus when those painful memories pop up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying about redirecting focus, but those negative moments just feel so much more real to me. Like when someone points out I'm quiet, it confirms all my worst fears about being awkward or boring. The good times don't stick in my mind the same way—they just feel like flukes.
therapist: Your voice sounds quieter and lower when you talk about those good moments—like they don’t carry the same weight for you, even though they happened. That makes so much sense—our brains are wired to hold onto painful experiences more tightly. What if we tried something small, like writing down one positive interaction each day to help balance that scale?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about focusing on positive moments, but it's hard to believe writing them down will make a difference. When I try to think about good interactions, they just feel small compared to all the negative stuff that weighs on me. It's like my brain automatically dismisses them as unimportant.
therapist: I hear the frustration in your voice—it’s higher and more intense right now, like you’re wrestling with this idea that the positive moments don’t "count" as much. That dismissive feeling is so common when we’re stuck in negative thought patterns. What if we tried framing it differently—not as "good vs bad" memories, but as practice in noticing when your brain might be discounting evidence that doesn’t fit the worry?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you’re saying, but it feels like those positive moments don’t stick. They’re fleeting, and then I’m right back into worrying about everything that’s wrong. It’s like my brain doesn’t want to let go of the bad stuff—it feels more real, more important somehow. I don’t know if reframing it will change that.
therapist: Your voice sounds both tired and a little shaky—like you’re caught between wanting to believe change is possible and feeling stuck in this pattern. That tug-of-war makes so much sense when our brains treat worries as urgent truths. What if we tried something small—just noticing when a positive moment happens, without pressuring yourself to "make it stick"? Even naming it quietly could be a start.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I can try noticing small positive moments, but part of me feels like it's pointless when the anxiety always comes rushing back anyway. It's like my brain immediately cancels out any good feeling with "but what if..." thoughts. I'm just so tired of this cycle.
therapist: Your voice sounds so weary—like you're carrying this heavy cycle of hope and disappointment. That exhaustion comes through clearly, especially when you describe how quickly the "what ifs" rush in. Let's honor that tiredness while also gently challenging it: what if the goal wasn't to stop the anxiety completely, but to create tiny moments of space between you and those thoughts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That makes sense in theory, but I don't know how to actually create that space. The anxiety feels so immediate and overwhelming—like it's glued to me. When you say "tiny moments," I worry I'll fail even at that small goal.
therapist: Your voice sounds both fragile and rushed—like you're bracing against this anxiety while also feeling worn down by it. That fear of "failing" at small goals is understandable, but what if we thought of it differently? Instead of measuring success, could we simply notice when the anxiety feels slightly less sticky, even for just a breath?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know...even noticing small changes feels like another thing I could fail at. Like if I try to pay attention and still feel awful, that just proves I'm bad at this too. The anxiety is so loud most days—it's exhausting trying to fight it or analyze it.
therapist: Your voice sounds both strained and tired—that mix of higher pitch and weariness tells me how much this struggle is weighing on you. It makes perfect sense that looking for small changes feels like setting yourself up for more disappointment when you're already exhausted. What if we took the pressure off completely? No "shoulds," no measuring—just noticing when the anxiety feels a tiny bit quieter, without needing to call it progress.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
